MUJAHID:v2p766/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p766/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p766/r1.claim: Mujahid says the night becomes even or settled.

FARRA:v3p273#2/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p273#2/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p273#2/r1.claim: Al-ḍuḥā means the entire day; sajā describes night as dark, still, and settled in its length, like a calm sea.

MAJAZ:v2p302/r1.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p302/r1.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p302/r1.claim: Sajā means became still; a quiet night is called sājin or sākinah.

MAJAZ:v2p302/r2.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p302/r2.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p302/r2.claim: The charioteer's line uses sājin for a quiet, still night.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p379/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p379/r2.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p379/r2.claim: Qatada says the night settles among people.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p379/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p379/r3.speaker: الحسن
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p379/r3.claim: Hasan says the night veils people when it arrives.

TUSTARI:93:2/r1.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:93:2/r1.speaker: author
TUSTARI:93:2/r1.claim: The night is the natural self becoming calm in the spirit’s company through continual remembrance of God.

TAB-FULL:v24p481#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p481#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس، الحسن، مجاهد، قتادة، الضحاك، ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v24p481#2/r3.claim: The reported glosses describe night as arriving, departing, becoming level, or settling and stilling the creatures.

TAB-FULL:v24p481#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p481#2/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p481#2/r4.claim: He prefers that night settle over its people and remain in darkness, like a calm sea; the root can describe stillness.

TAB-FULL:v24p484/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p484/r1.speaker: الأعشى، راجز
TAB-FULL:v24p484/r1.claim: Poetry uses sāj for a calm sea and describes a still night, supporting the author's preferred sense of settled stillness.

ZAJJAJ:v5p339/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p339/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p339/r1.claim: Ḍuḥā means daytime, or one period within the day.

ZAJJAJ:v5p339/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p339/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p339/r2.claim: Sajā means that the night became still; the poet’s al-layl al-sāj uses sāj for stillness.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3442#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3442#2/r1.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3442#2/r1.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr glosses the night as coming and covering everything.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3442#2/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3442#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3442#2/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas says the night has departed.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3442/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3442/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3442/r1.claim: Jundub reports that after the Prophet missed night prayer for one or two nights, a woman taunted him that his devil had left; the sura was revealed to reassure him that God had neither abandoned nor hated him.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3442/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3442/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3442/r2.claim: A second Jundub report says a stone injured the Prophet's finger; after two or three nights without rising, a woman said his devil had left, and the same verses were revealed.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3442/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3442/r3.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3442/r3.claim: Mujahid says the night has become still and settled.

NAHHAS:v5p249/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p249/r1.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p249/r1.claim: Sajā may be inclined even though its present is sajā yasjū because it shifts to yāʾ in sajayti.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r1.speaker: ابن كثير وعاصم وابن عامر
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r1.claim: Ibn Kathīr, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn ʿĀmir open the endings in this sūrah, al-Layl, and al-Ḍuḥā.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r2.speaker: الكسائي
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r2.claim: Al-Kisāʾī uses imālah throughout these endings and the endings of al-Layl and al-Ḍuḥā.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r3.speaker: حمزة
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r3.claim: Ḥamzah varies the endings: he inclines ḍuḥāhā but opens talāhā and ṭaḥāhā, while inclining the remaining forms, including sajā and daḥāhā.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r4.speaker: نافع
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r4.claim: Nāfiʿ has several transmissions: some make the endings intermediate, while Warsh and Qālūn are also reported to open them all; another report opens only talāhā and inclines the rest.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r5.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r5.speaker: أبو عمرو
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r5.claim: Abū ʿAmr is reported as using intermediate imālah, while ʿAbbās reports fully inclined forms for selected endings; other transmissions describe his treatment across verse endings.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r6.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r6.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r6.claim: Imālah is licensed where the alif behaves as one originating in yāʾ, as in derived verbs and nouns; an alif from wāw, such as العصا, normally resists it.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r7.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r7.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p418/r7.claim: Rare inclined examples with an alif from wāw are too uncommon to challenge the general pattern.

SULAMI:v2p400/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p400/r1.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v2p400/r1.claim: Dawn is the unveiling of the inner secret by God, while the servant is occupied with calling people through attention to creation.

SULAMI:v2p400/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p400/r2.speaker: الجنيد
SULAMI:v2p400/r2.claim: Dawn is the station of witnessing, and still night is the station of the inner eye associated with the Prophet's report that his heart is veiled.

THALABI:v10p223/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p223/r5.speaker: أهل المعاني
THALABI:v10p223/r5.claim: They understand both oaths with an implied 'Lord': by the Lord of morning and night.

THALABI:v10p223/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p223/r6.speaker: الحسن والعوفي عن ابن عباس
THALABI:v10p223/r6.claim: They say the night comes with its darkness.

THALABI:v10p223/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p223/r7.speaker: الوالبي عن ابن عباس
THALABI:v10p223/r7.claim: He interprets the night as having gone away.

THALABI:v10p223/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p223/r8.speaker: ضحاك
THALABI:v10p223/r8.claim: He says the night covers everything.

THALABI:v10p223/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p223/r9.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة وابن زيد
THALABI:v10p223/r9.claim: They say the night settles its darkness and stills the creatures; the expression also applies to a still night or sea.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p291#2/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p291#2/r5.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p291#2/r5.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr says the night draws near.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p291#2/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p291#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p291#2/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas says the night becomes dark.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p291#2/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p291#2/r7.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p291#2/r7.claim: Mujahid says the night becomes even or settled.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p291#2/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p291#2/r8.speaker: ابن حنطلة عن ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p291#2/r8.claim: Ibn Hantala reports from Ibn Abbas that the night has gone away.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p291#2/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p291#2/r9.speaker: عكرمة، عطاء، ابن زيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p291#2/r9.claim: Ikrima, Ata, and Ibn Zayd say the night quiets its creatures; the phrase derives from the sea becoming still, as a rajaz verse illustrates.

QUSHAYRI:v3p429/r3.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p429/r3.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p429/r3.claim: The still night may be the Night Journey, the general kind of night, the time of spiritual witnessing, or the night associated with the Prophet's report of a veil over his heart.

QUSHAYRI:v3p429/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p429/r4.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p429/r4.claim: Another interpretation relates the verse to God's descent to the lowest heaven at night, understood in a way compatible with divine attributes.

WAHIDI-QT:93:2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:93:2/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:93:2/r1.claim: Night becomes still among creation and settles in its darkness.

JISHUMI:v10p7449/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7449/r9.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7449/r9.claim: Sajw is stillness; the word describes a calm eye or sea. Two poetic lines use it for a still sea and a quiet night.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r1.speaker: جندب بن سفيان
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r1.claim: Jundub reports that after the Prophet was ill and missed two or three nights of prayer, a woman said his devil had left him; the verses were then revealed.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r2.speaker: قيل
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r2.claim: An alternative report identifies the woman who taunted the Prophet as Umm Jamil, the wife of Abu Lahab.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r3.speaker: المفسرون
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r3.claim: The commentators say Jews asked about Dhul-Qarnayn, the People of the Cave, and the Spirit; the Prophet promised an answer the next day without saying if God wills, so revelation paused.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r4.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r4.claim: Zayd says Gabriel's delay was caused by a puppy in the Prophet's house; Gabriel explained that angels do not enter a house with a dog or image.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r5.speaker: ابن جريج
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r5.claim: Ibn Jurayj gives the duration of the pause in revelation as twelve days.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas gives the duration of the pause in revelation as fifteen days.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r7.speaker: مقاتل
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r7.claim: Maqatil gives the duration of the pause in revelation as forty days.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r8.speaker: المشركون
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r8.claim: When the polytheists said Muhammad's Lord had abandoned and disliked him, God revealed this sura.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r9.speaker: جبريل
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p450/r9.claim: After the pause, the Prophet said he had missed Gabriel; Gabriel said he missed him even more but was an appointed servant, and the source links this to God's command governing revelation.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r1.claim: God swears by the whole daytime in al-duha, as the oath sets it against night; 7:98 likewise uses duha to mean daytime.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r2.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r2.claim: They interpret al-duha as the time when the sun has risen high and the day is temperate in heat and cold, summer and winter.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r3.speaker: الحسن
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r3.claim: Hasan says the night has come on with its darkness.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r4.speaker: العوفي عن ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r4.claim: Al-Awfi's report from Ibn Abbas takes the night phrase to mean that darkness has come on.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r5.speaker: الوالبي عن ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r5.claim: Al-Walibi's report from Ibn Abbas takes the night phrase to mean that it has departed.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r6.speaker: عطاء والضحاك
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r6.claim: Ata and al-Dahhak say night has covered everything with darkness.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r7.speaker: مجاهد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r7.claim: Mujahid interprets the night as having become level or even.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r8.speaker: قتادة وابن زيد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r8.claim: They say the night has become still and settled, with its darkness no longer increasing.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r9.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p454/r9.claim: The idiom layl saaj and bahr saaj describes a still night or sea.

KASHSHAF:93:2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:93:2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:93:2/r1.claim: Sajā describes darkness as settled and still.

KASHSHAF:93:2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:93:2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:93:2/r2.claim: A calm night may be called sājin; the root also describes settled sea waves and a steady, languid eye.

KASHSHAF:93:2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:93:2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:93:2/r3.claim: Another explanation is that people and sounds become quiet during the night.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p493#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p493#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p493#2/r3.claim: Saja most likely means the night became fully still and settled; other views say it arrived or passed.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p493#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p493#2/r4.speaker: الحارثي والأعشى
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p493#2/r4.claim: Two poems use the root in descriptions of a still night, calm sea, or steady gaze.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r1.claim: Five interpretations are given for sajā: it became dark; it departed, as transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās; it arrived, according to Saʿīd ibn Jubayr; it became still, according to several authorities; or its darkness extended, according to Ibn al-Aʿrābī.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r2.speaker: الفراء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r2.claim: On the meaning 'became still,' the darkness settled and grew long; sājin describes a calm, dark sea or night.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r3.speaker: أبو عبيدة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r3.claim: Arabic calls a night sājiya or sākinah, meaning still.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r4.speaker: الحادي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r4.claim: A cited poem praises the moon and a still night, using al-sāj as evidence for stillness.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r5.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r5.claim: Sajā means stillness when darkness reaches its fullness and settles.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r6.speaker: الماوردي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p156#2/r6.claim: Alternatively, stillness describes the creatures who settle during night.

RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r2.speaker: أبو عبيد والمبرد والزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r2.claim: They explain سجى as becoming still, as in a calm night, still eye, or sea whose waves have settled; a poetic line applies the word to the sea.

RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r3.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r3.claim: Al-Farraʾ explains سجى as becoming dark and settled through the night.

RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r4.speaker: الأصمعي وابن الأعرابي
RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r4.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿi and Ibn al-Aʿrabi explain the night as covering the day, like a person covered with a garment.

RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says night covers the world with darkness; in another report through Saʿid ibn Jubayr, its onset covers everything.

RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r6.speaker: الحسن
RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r6.claim: Al-Hasan says night clothes people in its darkness.

RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r7.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة والسدي وابن زيد
RAZI-FULL:v31p188/r7.claim: They explain the night as stilling people, either by metonymy or because its darkness has settled and become complete.

QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r10.speaker: الأصمعي
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r10.claim: Al-Asma'i explains the night covering as its veiling daytime, like a person covered with a garment.

QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r11.speaker: الحسن وابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r11.claim: Al-Hasan and Ibn Abbas say the night enveloped things in darkness; Ibn Abbas also glosses it as having gone or grown dark.

QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r12.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r12.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr says the night came on; a similar report is transmitted from Qatada.

QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r13.speaker: مجاهد عن ابن أبي نجيح
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r13.claim: Mujahid, through Ibn Abi Najih, interprets saja as becoming level or even.

QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r14.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r14.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r14.claim: The best-known linguistic reading is stillness: people settle during the night, or darkness settles evenly.

QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r5.speaker: قتادة ومجاهد وابن زيد وعكرمة
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r5.claim: Qatada, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, and Ikrima take saja to mean became still or calm, as in a quiet night, eye, or sea.

QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r6.speaker: الأعشى
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r6.claim: Al-A'sha's verse uses sajin of a calm sea to illustrate the stillness meaning.

QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r7.speaker: الراجز
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r7.claim: A rajaz poet calls the night al-saji, illustrating the calm-night sense.

QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r8.speaker: جرير
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r8.claim: Jarir uses sawaji for still eyes, another example of the settled sense.

QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r9.speaker: الضحاك
QURTUBI-FULL:93:1-3/r9.claim: Al-Dahhak says the night covered everything.

BAYDAWI-FULL:93:1-3/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:93:1-3/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:93:1-3/r2.claim: Night’s سجا means its people are quiet or its darkness settles; the earlier sura places night first by temporal origin, this one places day first by honor.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p344#7/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p344#7/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p344#7/r1.claim: The night 'settles' when people and sounds become quiet; the oath's response follows.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p495/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p495/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p495/r1.claim: Sajā can mean night departed or arrived; it also describes the calm moonlit night, still sea, and steady gaze. Al-Farrāʾ says it darkens and settles; Ibn al-Aʿrābī says its darkness intensifies.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p495/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p495/r2.speaker: الأعشى
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p495/r2.claim: Al-Aʿshā's poem uses sājin for a sea that is calm and still.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p495/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p495/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p495/r3.claim: The surah is Meccan and follows the previous mention of the most pious, the Prophet, by recounting God's favors to him.

SAMIN-DURR:93:2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:93:2/r1.speaker: الراغب
SAMIN-DURR:93:2/r1.claim: Al-Raghib says saja means to become still, as with settling sea waves, or slack as with an unfocused eye; the dead are figuratively ‘covered’ by a shroud.

SAMIN-DURR:93:2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:93:2/r2.speaker: الأعشى
SAMIN-DURR:93:2/r2.claim: Al-A‘sha’s poem contrasts a heaving sea with a still one, witnessing saja as calm or stillness.

SAMIN-DURR:93:2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:93:2/r3.speaker: الفراء
SAMIN-DURR:93:2/r3.claim: Al-Farra’ says saja means ‘grew dark’; Ibn al-A‘rabi intensifies this to ‘became very dark’, with a poem describing the moonlit, dark night.

SAMIN-DURR:93:2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:93:2/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:93:2/r4.claim: Other views take saja as receding, or as its opposite; the author notes the ambiguity without choosing between them.

SAMIN-DURR:93:2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:93:2/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:93:2/r5.claim: The root is one of the verbs with wāw; its final vowel is inclined for the rhyme, as with duha, which also comes from a wāw verb.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p424/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p424/r1.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p424/r1.claim: After the Prophet did not rise for one or two nights while ill, a woman accused his devil of abandoning him; the Prophet's report says the opening verses were then revealed.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p424/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p424/r2.speaker: مشركون
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p424/r2.claim: In another version, Gabriel's delay led the polytheists to say Muhammad had been abandoned, and the verses were revealed in response.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p424/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p424/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p424/r3.claim: Another narration says a stone injured the Prophet's finger, after which he stopped night worship for two or three nights and a woman made the same accusation; Ibn Kathir calls the injury report authentic but the causal link unusual.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p424/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p424/r4.speaker: ابن إسحاق
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p424/r4.claim: Ibn Ishaq says the woman who made the accusation was Umm Jamil, the wife of Abu Lahab.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p425/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p425/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p425/r2.claim: God swears by the forenoon and its light, and by night when it settles, darkens, and grows still.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p425/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p425/r3.speaker: مجاهد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p425/r3.claim: Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd explain saja as night becoming still, dark, and deep.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p425/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p425/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p425/r4.claim: The contrasting light of day and darkness of night visibly demonstrate the Creator's power.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p452/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p452/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p452/r2.claim: Sajā can mean that night’s people become still or that its darkness, covering, and blackness settle evenly; al-mustajī means covered.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p452/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p452/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p452/r3.claim: The alternation of mixed and pure light and darkness can represent Qur’anic clear and ambiguous teachings and human spiritual conditions.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p452/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p452/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p452/r4.claim: The heart’s light can overcome the soul’s darkness, while appetite can darken the whole person; spirit or temperament then elevates or degrades the person.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p452/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p452/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p452/r5.claim: When spirit dominates temperament, a person rises beyond the rank of angels; when temperament dominates, a person falls below beasts.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p452/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p452/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p452/r6.claim: When temperament dominates, a person falls below the rank of beasts.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p454/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p454/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p454/r2.claim: The opening’s hidden night recalls uncertainty about one’s path and destiny; remembering the signs and seeking refuge in God bring certainty.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p455/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p455/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p455/r1.claim: The opening night evokes the beginning’s obscurity, while the manifest day evokes the clarity reached by people whose hearts God has strengthened.

DURR-FULL:v8p539/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p539/r4.speaker: جندب البجلي
DURR-FULL:v8p539/r4.claim: When the Prophet was ill and did not rise at night for two or three nights, a woman taunted him that his devil had abandoned him; the opening verses answered her.

DURR-FULL:v8p539/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p539/r7.speaker: جندب
DURR-FULL:v8p539/r7.claim: After a stone injured his finger and the Prophet stopped night prayer for two or three nights, a woman blamed his devil's departure; al-Tirmidhi authenticated the report.

DURR-FULL:v8p540/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p540/r1.speaker: زيد بن أرقم
DURR-FULL:v8p540/r1.claim: After Abu Lahab's surah, his wife confronted the Prophet; when revelation paused and she said his companion had abandoned and hated him, the opening verses were revealed.

DURR-FULL:v8p540/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p540/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن شداد
DURR-FULL:v8p540/r2.claim: He reports Khadija saying that the Prophet's Lord seemed to have rejected him, after which the verses were revealed.

DURR-FULL:v8p540/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p540/r3.speaker: عروة
DURR-FULL:v8p540/r3.claim: When Gabriel was delayed and the Prophet became distressed, Khadija inferred from his distress that God had rejected him; the surah followed.

DURR-FULL:v8p540/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p540/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p540/r5.claim: After revelation paused for days, polytheists taunted that God had abandoned Muhammad; the passage came down, and the night ‘when it settles’ means when it arrives.

DURR-FULL:v8p540/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p540/r6.speaker: قتادة والضحاك
DURR-FULL:v8p540/r6.claim: Their mursal reports give the same occasion: a pause in revelation prompted the claim that God had abandoned Muhammad, answered by this passage.

DURR-FULL:v8p540/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p540/r7.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v8p540/r7.claim: He glossed the midmorning light as an hour of daylight and the night as quiet among people.

DURR-FULL:v8p541/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p541/r1.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v8p541/r1.claim: He glossed the night as becoming level or settled.

DURR-FULL:v8p541/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p541/r2.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v8p541/r2.claim: He glossed the night as covering people.

DURR-FULL:v8p541/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p541/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p541/r3.claim: He glossed the night as arriving.

DURR-FULL:v8p541/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p541/r4.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
DURR-FULL:v8p541/r4.claim: He said the night arrives and covers everything.

DURR-FULL:v8p541/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p541/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p541/r5.claim: In another report the night has departed; God has neither left nor hated the Prophet.

DURR-FULL:v8p541/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p541/r6.speaker: أم حفص
DURR-FULL:v8p541/r6.claim: A dead puppy hidden beneath the Prophet's bed delayed revelation for four days; after Khawla found it, the Prophet trembled and the passage through ‘you will be satisfied’ came down.

BURSEVI:v10p349#3/r10.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p349#3/r10.speaker: جعفر الصادق
BURSEVI:v10p349#3/r10.claim: Ja‘far al-Sadiq identifies the duha with the morning when God spoke to Moses and the night with the Night Journey.

BURSEVI:v10p349#3/r11.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p349#3/r11.speaker: صاحب كشف الأسرار
BURSEVI:v10p349#3/r11.claim: Kashf al-Asrar reads day and night as disclosure and veiling, signs of the breeze of divine gentleness and the scorching wind of divine severity, and of beauty's lights and majesty's traces.

BURSEVI:v10p349#3/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p349#3/r8.speaker: ابن خالويه
BURSEVI:v10p349#3/r8.claim: Ibn Khalawayh treats night as conjoined to duha rather than as an oath, since it could be preceded by thumma or fa, neither of which introduces an oath.

BURSEVI:v10p349#3/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p349#3/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p349#3/r9.claim: Saja can mean that the inhabitants grow quiet, by attributing their action to the time, or that darkness settles and reaches its full intensity before beginning to recede; the word also describes a calm sea or windless night.

BURSEVI:v10p350/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p350/r1.speaker: الجنيد
BURSEVI:v10p350/r1.claim: Al-Junayd calls duha the station of witnessing and the settled night the station of ghayn, the clouding over the heart mentioned in a Prophetic report.

BURSEVI:v10p350/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p350/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p350/r2.claim: A Persian couplet treats duha as the brightness of the Prophet's face and night as the darkness of his hair.

BURSEVI:v10p350/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p350/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p350/r3.claim: Night precedes in the preceding surah because darkness is the original state: day arises with the sun and the air returns to its first state when it sets; day leads here because of its intrinsic and incidental honor.

BURSEVI:v10p350/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p350/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p350/r4.claim: Although duha is only one hour and night spans many, it equals the whole night as Muhammad equals all prophets; joy is brief while worldly sorrow and anxiety last longer.

BURSEVI:v10p350/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p350/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p350/r5.claim: A report says a black cloud over the Throne's left side rained grief for three hundred years, while a white cloud on the right rained joy for only an hour, explaining why sorrow is common and lasting and joy rare.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r1.claim: The verse swears by the night as a genus, when its people are still; this may be a figurative attribution or an understood reference to its people.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r10.claim: Some jurists count a severe nighttime wind as an excuse for missing congregational prayer.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r11.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r11.claim: They take the oath's ḍuḥā as the time God spoke to Moses and its night as the Night Journey.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r12.speaker: بعض الناس
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r12.claim: Some allegorically identify ḍuḥā with the Prophet's face and night with his hair.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r2.speaker: قتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r2.claim: He explains the phrase as people and sounds becoming quiet, usually after some time has passed in the night.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r3.claim: Another explanation is that darkness settles without perceptible increase or change; the word first described calm sea waves, as al-Aʿshā's verse illustrates.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r4.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r4.claim: He says سجا الليل means that night darkness became intense.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r5.speaker: ابن جبير
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r5.claim: He glosses the night as approaching and covering everything.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r6.claim: One transmission from Ibn Abbas gives a gloss without mentioning the covering of everything; another says سجا means that night passed.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r7.claim: A separate report from him says the night passed, a sense the author calls contrary to the common explanation.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r8.claim: In ordinary Arabic, a calm or still night means a night without wind; this is a conventional description of the night itself.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p153#3/r9.claim: Night is a time, so stillness is not literal motionlessness; ordinary usage speaks of it as still because air or wind is imperceptible or absent.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r1.speaker: الإمام
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r1.claim: The Imam sees no reason to rule out the allegory that ḍuḥā is the Prophet's face and night his hair.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r10.claim: One consolation reads the alternating day and night as analogous to revelation's descent and pause: neither reflects divine desire or rejection, since both occur for wisdom.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r11.claim: Another consolation points to day and night alternately prevailing and says the Prophet should not expect to be free from people's words.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r12.claim: The previous consolatory analogies assume ḍuḥā means the whole day and night means the whole night.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r13.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r13.claim: Some explain the specified dark night as the time when a lover meets the beloved safely away from informers and watchers.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r14.speaker: الطيبي
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r14.claim: Al-Tibi says the oath invokes the two times of the Prophet's prayers, which brought him delight and greater closeness.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r15.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r15.claim: A marfūʿ report cited by al-Tibi says sacrifice was prescribed for the Prophet, and ḍuḥā prayer was commanded to him but not to the community.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r16.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r16.speaker: الطيبي
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r16.claim: Al-Tibi links night to the Prophet's extra night prayer, which refutes claims that God had rejected or forsaken him.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r2.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r2.claim: Another allegory makes ḍuḥā the male members of the Prophet's household and night its women.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r3.speaker: الإمام
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r3.claim: He suggests ḍuḥā may symbolize the Prophet's mission and night the pause in revelation, which brought loneliness after intimacy.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r4.speaker: الإمام
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r4.claim: He also suggests divine knowledge that exposes hidden things and divine pardon that conceals defects.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r5.speaker: الإمام
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r5.claim: Other possible allusions are Islam's rise and later return to strangeness, or intellect's perfection and death.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r6.speaker: الإمام
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r6.claim: He also proposes the Prophet's flawless public conduct and a private self beyond defect in the knowledge of the unseen.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r7.claim: These are allusive interpretations rather than tafsir proper; the symbolic and spiritual mode admits still more possibilities.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r8.claim: Ḍuḥā precedes night here because its greater light is honorable, existent, beneficial, and akin to the angelic realm.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p154/r9.claim: Night preceded day in the previous sūra because darkness, as privation, is the basis from which later light appears; another explanation contrasts Abū Bakr's prior unbelief with the Prophet's.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p155/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p155/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p155/r1.claim: The quoted poetic image is praised as something appreciated by people of spiritual taste.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p155/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p155/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p155/r2.claim: The oath by night may follow the same allusive pattern as Qatada's interpretation, as may some interpretations of the two oaths together.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p155/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p155/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p155/r3.claim: If ḍuḥā is the familiar daylight interval and night the whole night, an hour of day is compared to the whole night as the Prophet is to all prophets.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p155/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p155/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p155/r4.claim: Another interpretation contrasts daytime joy with nighttime distress and says worldly worries endure longer than happiness.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p155/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p155/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p155/r5.claim: A story says clouds over the Throne's left side poured grief for three hundred years, while a white cloud on the right poured joy for an hour; the author leaves its reliability to God.

ELMALILI:93:2-4#2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:93:2-4#2/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:93:2-4#2/r3.claim: Abandonment can express either grace or chastisement; the contrast of forenoon and night hints that the Prophet remains under divine mercy, while the denial of hatred excludes wrath.

ELMALILI:93:2-4/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r1.claim: The phrase can describe the settled middle of night, after some time has elapsed, when darkness has reached its depth, covers what it will, and silence falls.

ELMALILI:93:2-4/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r10.claim: This stillness includes physical and spiritual relief, rest from distress, or the passing of grief as night ends.

ELMALILI:93:2-4/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r11.claim: Night can symbolize life's suffering, death's grief, cessation of revelation and knowledge, and spiritual constriction; here the focus is respite during that darkness or the joy that comes when revelation resumes.

ELMALILI:93:2-4/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r12.claim: Duha expresses the bright, youthful joy of life and revealed knowledge, while the settled night signals rest before a promised renewal; this relation fittingly introduces the assurance that the Lord has not abandoned Muhammad.

ELMALILI:93:2-4/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r2.claim: Other possibilities are the onset of darkness and covering, the stilling of the wind, or the night drawing to an end; each contrasts or corresponds with duha as grief, joy, or grief's passing.

ELMALILI:93:2-4/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r3.claim: Sajā derives from sujuww, meaning for something to settle and become still; bahr sājī is calm sea, tarf sājī a still eye, and layl sājī a quiet, windless night.

ELMALILI:93:2-4/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r4.claim: The same root yields sajiyya for a settled disposition and tasjiya for covering, so the night may be understood as quiet, fully dark and covering, or passing away.

ELMALILI:93:2-4/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r5.speaker: ابن عربي
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r5.claim: Ibn Arabi says the night has become intensely dark.

ELMALILI:93:2-4/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r6.speaker: İbn Cübeyr
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r6.claim: Ibn Jubayr is cited as saying that the night arrives and covers everything.

ELMALILI:93:2-4/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r7.speaker: İbn Abbâs
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r7.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas through the Awfi route explains sajā as the night coming on.

ELMALILI:93:2-4/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r8.speaker: İbn Abbâs
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r8.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas explains sajā as the night having gone away.

ELMALILI:93:2-4/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:93:2-4/r9.claim: The majority's basic meaning is stillness and rest, not the force of darkness; the familiar calm, windless night supports this, as does the verse saying night is for rest.

QUTB-ZILAL:93:2/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:93:2/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:93:2/r1.claim: The wording, rhythm, and scene spread tenderness, mercy, acceptance, and delicate sorrow; the quiet, clear night is chosen rather than night’s general darkness, then dawn reveals the scene.

QUTB-ZILAL:93:2/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:93:2/r2.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:93:2/r2.claim: The peaceful cosmic frame invites meditation and communion with creation and its Creator; the oath’s purpose is to make the Prophet feel at home and not abandoned.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p394#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p394#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p394#2/r1.claim: The oath rebuts the idolaters' claim that revelation stopped when the Prophet did not recite the Quran at night for several days; the warning targets their insinuation, since the Prophet himself had no doubt.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p394#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p394#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p394#2/r2.claim: Morning brightness evokes revelation and guidance, while night evokes the Prophet's Quran recitation that nearby idolaters heard; the time when night settled may be when he prayed, as in al-Muzzammil.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p394#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p394#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p394#2/r5.claim: سجا means night extended and lengthened its darkness, in two cited vocal forms, like a person entirely covered by a blanket; its root is wāw but it is written like الضحى for the same orthographic reason.

ASAD-NOTES:93:1#n1/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:93:1#n1/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:93:1#n1/r1.claim: The brief, intermittent happiness of morning contrasts with the much longer sorrows of life, as in 90:4.

ASAD-NOTES:93:1#n1/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:93:1#n1/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:93:1#n1/r2.claim: As morning follows night, divine mercy will relieve every suffering in this life or the next; God has willed grace and mercy for Himself.

BINTSHATI:v1p24/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p24/r1.speaker: ابن قيم الجوزية
BINTSHATI:v1p24/r1.claim: The prevailing earlier view treats Qur'anic oaths as glorifying what is sworn by, since created things are great signs.

BINTSHATI:v1p24/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p24/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p24/r2.claim: Reading the night oath as glorification can require strained interpretations because night can also evoke loneliness, death, graves, and estrangement.

BINTSHATI:v1p24/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p24/r4.speaker: الشيخ محمد عبده
BINTSHATI:v1p24/r4.claim: Abduh likens night to divine majesty through its fearful stilling power, while also noting its benefits for bodily and mental rest.

BINTSHATI:v1p24/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p24/r5.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p24/r5.claim: The author finds this search for grandeur in night forced by an assumed rule that every oath must glorify its object.

BINTSHATI:v1p25/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p25/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p25/r1.claim: Earlier interpreters explain night in general, although the verse specifically qualifies it as the night when it settles.

BINTSHATI:v1p25/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p25/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p25/r2.claim: The author argues that interpreters conflate glorification with the wisdom of creation; every created thing has wisdom, which alone does not establish an oath's intended grandeur.

BINTSHATI:v1p25/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p25/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p25/r3.claim: The oath's wāw can serve a rhetorical purpose beyond glorification: strongly directing attention to familiar sensory realities that prepare the reader for unseen meanings.

BINTSHATI:v1p25/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p25/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p25/r4.claim: The quality selected for the oath suits its context; any impression of glorification strengthens the attention rather than defining the device's main purpose.

BINTSHATI:v1p26/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p26/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p26/r1.claim: The daily alternation from bright duha to a quiet night is a sensory image that prepares for the unseen pause in revelation, without suggesting that heaven abandoned earth.

BINTSHATI:v1p26/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p26/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p26/r2.claim: The sensory contrast between light and darkness can clarify unseen guidance and truth or misguidance and falsehood.

BINTSHATI:v1p26/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p26/r3.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي ونظام الدين النيسابوري
BINTSHATI:v1p26/r3.claim: They compare alternating night and day, which wax and wane by wisdom, to revelation being sent and withheld according to divine purposes.

BINTSHATI:v1p27/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p27/r1.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي ونظام الدين النيسابوري
BINTSHATI:v1p27/r1.claim: They also say the oath answers the disbelievers' taunt: they were unable to prove their claim that God had abandoned Muhammad.

BINTSHATI:v1p27/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p27/r2.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي ونظام الدين النيسابوري
BINTSHATI:v1p27/r2.claim: A further interpretation compares night and day alternately prevailing to how no created people are exempt from such change.

BINTSHATI:v1p27/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p27/r3.speaker: الشيخ محمد عبده
BINTSHATI:v1p27/r3.claim: Abduh says the Prophet's distress during the pause was relieved by renewed revelation: duha represents life-giving first revelation, while quiet night restores strength for later work.

BINTSHATI:v1p27/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p27/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p27/r4.claim: The author's sensory analogy is nearly lost in Abduh's account of night as rest and preparation for work.

BINTSHATI:v1p27/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p27/r5.speaker: ابن قيم الجوزية
BINTSHATI:v1p27/r5.claim: Ibn al-Qayyim comes close to matching the bright duha after darkness with revelation after its pause, but frames the oath as proof of God's lordship, wisdom, and mercy.

BINTSHATI:v1p28/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p28/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p28/r1.claim: The author says Ibn al-Qayyim's appeal to doubts about God's lordship misses the stated occasion, which concerns a claim that God abandoned Muhammad.

BINTSHATI:v1p28/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p28/r2.speaker: بعض المفسرين
BINTSHATI:v1p28/r2.claim: Some interpret the order of duha then night as preferring life until believers reach maturity, avoiding despair first and then fear of divine plotting.

BINTSHATI:v1p28/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p28/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p28/r3.claim: The author finds no clear connection between the oath and its answer in the accounts of al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, and Abu Hayyan, and notes they do not compare it with God's explicit denials of oaths.

BINTSHATI:v1p28/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p28/r4.speaker: الطبري
BINTSHATI:v1p28/r4.claim: Al-Tabari reports disagreements over whether duha means the whole day or one daytime hour, and whether saja means night arriving, departing, settling, or becoming still.

BINTSHATI:v1p29/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p29/r1.speaker: الطبري
BINTSHATI:v1p29/r1.claim: Al-Tabari selects daylight, understood as visible sunlight, for duha and stillness among its people for saja.

BINTSHATI:v1p29/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p29/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
BINTSHATI:v1p29/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhshari defines duha as the early day when the sun rises and shines, while also reporting that it can mean the whole day; saja is settled darkness or quiet people and sounds.

BINTSHATI:v1p29/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p29/r3.speaker: أبو حيان
BINTSHATI:v1p29/r3.claim: Abu Hayyan says saja may mean night departing or arriving.

BINTSHATI:v1p29/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p29/r4.speaker: الفراء وابن الأعرابي
BINTSHATI:v1p29/r4.claim: Al-Farra says saja means that night darkened and rested, while Ibn al-A'rabi says its darkness intensified.

BINTSHATI:v1p29/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p29/r5.speaker: النيسابوري
BINTSHATI:v1p29/r5.claim: Al-Nisaburi allows saja to mean that people become still, a figurative attribution to night.

BINTSHATI:v1p29/r6.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p29/r6.speaker: الشيخ محمد عبده
BINTSHATI:v1p29/r6.claim: Abduh defines duha as sunlight in the day's prime and saja as the quiet and inactivity of night-time inhabitants.

BINTSHATI:v1p29/r7.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p29/r7.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p29/r7.claim: Although the words can carry several lexical senses, the rhetoric of this particular setting admits only the single sense that best fits it.

BINTSHATI:v1p31/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p31/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p31/r1.claim: The appointment of people at duha in 20:59 and its use opposite evening in 79:46 show that duha means a specific daytime period, not the whole day; the same reading fits the sun's duha in 91:1.

BINTSHATI:v1p31/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p31/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p31/r2.claim: Saja means the lull or stillness of night, not its arrival or departure; its contrast with duha and Arabic uses of the root support this sense.

BINTSHATI:v1p31/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p31/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
BINTSHATI:v1p31/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says duha was chosen because it was when God spoke to Moses and when Moses met the sorcerers; the author rejects this anachronistic reading because the cited passages were revealed much later.

BINTSHATI:v1p32/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p32/r1.speaker: النيسابوري والرازي
BINTSHATI:v1p32/r1.claim: Al-Nisaburi and al-Razi liken the duha hour to the whole night, just as Muhammad is said to equal all prophets and their communities.

BINTSHATI:v1p32/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p32/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p32/r2.claim: The author excludes esoteric readings that turn duha and night into the Prophet's face and hair, male and female relatives, knowledge and forgiveness, or Islam's rise and later estrangement.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p353/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p353/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p353/r1.claim: Sūrat al-Ḍuḥā and the following Sūrah Alam Nashraḥ form a pair assuring the Prophet of success; the former reflects intense Makkan opposition, the latter emerging signs of success.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p353/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p353/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p353/r2.claim: The discourse moves from day and night as models of developmental trials, to reassurance, promised better times, examples of past divine help, and duties arising from those favours.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p355/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p355/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p355/r2.claim: Sajā means becoming still; the oath points to the quiet, restful part of night, paired with the corresponding daytime period.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p356/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p356/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p356/r1.claim: Day and night complement one another as divine mercy: night gives rest and day permits seeking bounty, sustaining the world together.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:93:1/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:93:1/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:93:1/r3.claim: Night refers to the time when the Prophet recited the Qur'an aloud at home or near the Kaaba and polytheists secretly listened.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p409/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p409/r4.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p409/r4.claim: Sajā has three senses: becoming still, growing deeply dark, and covering something, as in shrouding a dead body.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p410/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p410/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p410/r1.claim: Sajā brings together stillness and darkness, matching revelation's suspension and loss of light; yaghshā and yasri imply movement and therefore fit less well.

STUDYQURAN:93:1/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:93:1/r1.speaker: others
STUDYQURAN:93:1/r1.claim: Some identify morning brightness with the morning God spoke to Moses and night with the Night Journey and Ascension; others identify it as the moment Moses' opponents recognized truth and prostrated.

STUDYQURAN:93:1/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:93:1/r3.speaker: others
STUDYQURAN:93:1/r3.claim: Other symbolic readings make morning the Garden's light and night the Fire's darkness, or light in knowers' hearts and blackness in disbelievers' hearts.

STUDYQURAN:93:1/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:93:1/r4.speaker: Sh and Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:93:1/r4.claim: “When still” may describe darkness spreading across the day; night may also mean as it approaches or as it leaves.

STUDYQURAN:93:1/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:93:1/r5.speaker: Sh and Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:93:1/r5.claim: The night is also interpreted as the night approaching or departing.

STUDYQURAN:93:intro/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:93:intro/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:93:intro/r1.claim: Al-Ḍuḥā is early Makkan and ranked fourth by many, seventh by others; it may be the first sūrah revealed whole, though others give that distinction to al-Fātiḥah.

STUDYQURAN:93:intro/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:93:intro/r3.speaker: several commentators
STUDYQURAN:93:intro/r3.claim: One occasion account says revelation paused for twelve, forty, or fifty days, after which an idolater taunted Muhammad that his satan had forsaken him, prompting reassurance.

STUDYQURAN:93:intro/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:93:intro/r4.speaker: others
STUDYQURAN:93:intro/r4.claim: Another account says idolaters declared that Muhammad's Lord had forsaken and despised him.

STUDYQURAN:93:intro/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:93:intro/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:93:intro/r5.claim: A further account says illness kept the Prophet from night vigil for two or three nights; Umm Jamīl, Abū Lahab's wife, taunted him, and vv. 1–3 were revealed.

STUDYQURAN:93:intro/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:93:intro/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:93:intro/r6.claim: The sūrah consoles the Prophet: it assures him God will not abandon him, recalls God's favors, and ends by urging care for the downtrodden and preaching the message.

STUDYQURAN:94:intro/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:94:intro/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:94:intro/r3.claim: Some say Sūrahs 93 and 94 were originally one, since Companions recited them together in one prayer cycle without a basmalah separating them.

STUDYQURAN:94:intro/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:94:intro/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:94:intro/r5.claim: Both sūrahs present God's bounties as relief: Sūrah 93 addresses external needs, Sūrah 94 spiritual relief; 94 recalls blessings, reassures, then commands exertion and turning to God.
